When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?

Kaifei Wang ††thanks: Peking University. Email: {wkf5094,shanzikang}@stu.pku.edu.cn, wanglw@pku.edu.cn.    Zikang Shan11footnotemark: 1    Liwei Wang11footnotemark: 1    Yinyu Ye ††thanks: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, SIMIS, and Stanford University. Email: yinyu-ye@stanford.edu.    Han Zhong ††thanks: Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Email: han.zhong@sjtu.edu.cn.
Abstract

Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training. Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, where the EMA coefficient β\beta controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly, we prove that increasing β\beta within a range that prevents overshoot strictly accelerates optimization. When gradients are estimated from sampled responses, a positive expected gain can be obscured by sampling fluctuations. We show that as the learning rate η\eta decreases, the expected gain with fixed β\beta vanishes faster than these fluctuations, whereas increasing β\beta to keep η/(1−β)\eta/(1-\beta) within the safe regime preserves a nonvanishing gain that eventually dominates them. Bandit simulations quantitatively validate these predictions. RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base using SGD with EMA and AdamW support our principle of choosing larger coefficients in practical LLM post-training. On Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, simply increasing β1\beta_{1} improves mean validation accuracy by nearly 22 percentage points over the conventional choice, demonstrating the principle’s effectiveness at a larger model scale.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an important approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) (Lambert et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025). In RLVR, responses are sampled from the current policy and evaluated using verifiable rewards, so the training data distribution evolves as the policy changes. This differs from pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, which optimize next-token prediction (NTP) on given text sequences (Brown et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022). Despite these differences, RLVR commonly adopts Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) or AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019), together with conventional first-moment momentum settings (Zhang et al., 2025; Mukherjee et al., 2026). The design and configuration of optimizers for RLVR have received relatively limited attention.

One important aspect of optimizer design and configuration is the use of first-moment momentum, implemented in Adam and AdamW as an exponential moving average (EMA) of past gradients. While EMA has shown empirical benefits in NTP training (Chen et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025), Mukherjee et al. (2026) report that momentum does not consistently improve performance in their RLVR experiments and can even reduce it under a conventional choice of the momentum coefficient. These observations motivate a closer examination of whether EMA can benefit RLVR and what factors influence its effectiveness.

To understand when EMA benefits RLVR and how to choose its coefficient, we adopt a KL-regularized response-level bandit formulation (Xiong et al., 2024). We analyze natural policy gradient (NPG, Kakade, 2001) with a softmax policy parameterization and bias-corrected EMA. NPG provides a tractable theoretical framework for studying policy improvement while controlling changes in the policy distribution, a principle shared by TRPO and PPO (Schulman et al., 2015; Schulman et al., 2017; Shani et al., 2020). NPG-based analysis has also provided practical guidance for LLM post-training (Gai et al., 2026, e.g., ). Our contributions are as follows.

Deterministic acceleration and stochastic gains. We first prove that, with exact gradients, increasing the EMA coefficient within a safe regime strictly accelerates optimization, which appears to contrast with the limited benefits reported in prior RLVR experiments (Mukherjee et al., 2026). A deterministic gain, however, need not translate into a consistent improvement when gradients are estimated from sampled responses, as sampling fluctuations may obscure the benefit. We characterize the expectation and variance of the objective gain and prove that, for a fixed EMA coefficient, the expected gain remains positive for sufficiently small learning rates but vanishes faster than the sampling fluctuations as the learning rate decreases (Theorems 4.2 and 5.3).

Principled selection of momentum coefficients. We next show that scaling the EMA coefficient β\beta with the learning rate η\eta so that η/(1−β)\eta/(1-\beta) is a positive constant within the safe regime yields a nonvanishing expected gain that eventually dominates sampling fluctuations (Theorem 5.4). We further prove that an appropriately increased coefficient allows a smaller learning rate to achieve comparable expected performance under the same update and sample budgets, with asymptotically lower variance of the objective value (Theorem 5.5).

Validation in bandits and LLM post-training. We quantitatively validate the predicted gain and fluctuation scales in numerical bandit experiments. GRPO experiments (Shao et al., 2024) on Qwen3-4B-Base (Yang et al., 2025) support our theoretical predictions in practical LLM post-training with both SGD with EMA and the widely used AdamW optimizer: larger coefficients improve performance and, when paired with smaller learning rates, yield more stable training with comparable or slightly improved performance. We further demonstrate the principle’s effectiveness at a larger model scale: on Qwen2.5-32B (Qwen et al., 2024), simply increasing AdamW’s first-moment coefficient improves mean validation accuracy by nearly 22 percentage points over the conventional choice.

2 Related work

Optimization and momentum in RLVR. Recent work revisits optimizer design for RLVR through momentum-based normalization (Zhang et al., 2025), spectral transformations (Fan et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026), and parameter-space exploration (Venkatkrishna et al., 2026). Focusing on optimizer momentum, Fontana et al. (2026) analyze how accumulated AdamW momentum can continue driving updates after clipping suppresses the current policy-gradient contribution during repeated optimization of the same batch. Most directly related to our motivation, Mukherjee et al. (2026) find that SGD can match or outperform AdamW and report no consistent benefit from momentum. Motivated by these empirical findings, we study how the benefit of ordinary EMA momentum in RLVR depends on the momentum coefficient, learning rate, and sampling noise.

Momentum in reinforcement learning. Prior work studies momentum for accelerating policy optimization and reducing gradient-estimation error in conventional RL. Chen et al. (2024) establish accelerated convergence for exact-gradient policy optimization under tabular softmax parameterization using Nesterov momentum with a restart rule. Momentum-based variance reduction has also been studied for policy gradient (Huang et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2022) and natural policy gradient (Feng et al., 2024). Huang et al. (2022) develop Bregman policy optimization with basic momentum and a variance-reduced variant. This literature primarily concerns convergence and sample complexity in conventional RL, with reported experiments on control and Atari benchmarks. We study bias-corrected averaging of past natural gradients in a KL-regularized RLVR bandit model, comparing objective values with and without momentum and examining the practical implications through GRPO experiments with language models.

Momentum in supervised learning and stochastic optimization. Analyses of online learning and general stochastic optimization characterize regimes in which momentum behaves similarly to SGD under appropriate learning-rate scaling (Yuan et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2024). In language-model pretraining, AdEMAMix combines fast and slow gradient averages to exploit longer gradient memory (Pagliardini et al., 2025), while ADana combines time-varying momentum schedules with a direct gradient term and damping (Ferbach et al., 2026). These pretraining studies concern next-token prediction on given text sequences. Our focus is momentum in RLVR, where reward feedback is obtained from responses sampled from the evolving policy.

3 Preliminaries

In this section, we introduce the model, algorithms, and notation used throughout the paper, providing the foundation for our theoretical analysis.

3.1 Model and parameterization

Basic Setup. Let x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} be a given input prompt, and let y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y} be a corresponding response generated by the language model. The model is parameterized as a policy π\pi characterized by θ\theta, from which responses are sampled y∼πθ(⋅∣x)y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x). Each prompt-response pair (x,y)(x,y) is evaluated by a verifier and receives a reward r⁡(x,y)r(x,y). We consider the case of deterministic binary rewards: r⁡(x,y)r(x,y) is 1 if and only if the response yy is a correct answer to the prompt xx, and 0 otherwise. Let 𝐫∈{0,1}|𝒴|\mathbf{r}\in\{0,1\}^{|\mathcal{Y}|} denote the vector of rewards for all possible responses to the prompt xx. We maximize the expected reward while penalizing divergence from a fixed reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, using the objective

J(θ)=𝔼y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[r(x,y)]−γKL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥πref(⋅∣x)),J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}[r(x,y)]-\gamma\operatorname{KL}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)), (3.1)

where KL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥πref(⋅∣x)):=∑y∈𝒴πθ(y∣x)log(πθ(y∣x)/πref(y∣x))\operatorname{KL}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)):=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\log(\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)/\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)) is the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the policy πθ(⋅∣x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) and the reference policy, and γ>0\gamma>0 is a regularization coefficient. Assume πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is a full-support policy. To exclude degenerate cases, we assume that the initial policy is suboptimal and that the response set contains both correct and incorrect responses. The objective J⁡(θ)J(\theta) encourages higher expected reward while penalizing deviations from a fixed reference policy, such as one obtained through supervised fine-tuning.

Policy parameterization. We adopt the standard softmax parameterization to model response generation. Given a prompt xx, we parameterize the conditional distribution over responses using a logit vector θ∈ℝ|𝒴|\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{Y}|} as πθ​(y∣x)=eθ⁡(x,y)/∑y′∈𝒴eθ⁡(x,y′)\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)=e^{\theta(x,y)}/\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}e^{\theta(x,y^{\prime})}, where θ⁡(x,y)\theta(x,y) is the logit score for response yy given prompt xx. This response-level softmax parameterization provides a tractable abstraction of autoregressive generation in modern LLMs, whose token-level policies use softmax distributions (Ziegler et al., 2019; Zhong et al., 2025).

3.2 Training dynamics

Natural policy gradient. Our theoretical analysis focuses on the natural policy gradient (NPG) method, which preconditions the policy gradient using the Fisher information matrix (Kakade, 2001). Let θt\theta_{t} denote the parameter vector at iteration tt and πθt(⋅∣x)\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot\mid x) the induced policy. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly, the NPG update is given by:

θt+1=θt+ηℱ†(θt)∇J(θt),ℱ(θ)=𝔼y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[∇logπθ(y∣x)∇logπθ(y∣x)⊤].\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}+\eta\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}(\theta_{t})\nabla J(\theta_{t}),\qquad\mathcal{F}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\nabla\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\nabla\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)^{\top}\right]. (3.2)

Here η>0\eta>0 represents the learning rate, ℱ⁡(θ)\mathcal{F}(\theta) is the Fisher information matrix, and ℱ†​(θ)\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}(\theta) is its Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. When policy gradients are estimated from sampled responses, we replace the gradient ∇J​(⋅)\nabla J(\cdot) with its unbiased estimator ∇J^​(⋅)\widehat{\nabla J}(\cdot), which uses a batch of sampled responses to approximate the expected reward, while the KL gradient and the Fisher information matrix are computed exactly. Specifically, let θ^t\widehat{\theta}_{t} be the parameter vector under the sampled NPG update. The update is given by:

θ^t+1=θ^t+η​ℱ†​(θ^t)​∇J^​(θ^t).\widehat{\theta}_{t+1}=\widehat{\theta}_{t}+\eta\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}(\widehat{\theta}_{t})\widehat{\nabla J}(\widehat{\theta}_{t}). (3.3)

NPG not only enjoys favorable convergence guarantees under softmax parameterization (Agarwal et al., 2021; Cen et al., 2022), but also connects to modern RL algorithms used in LLM post-training. It can be viewed as maximizing a linearized objective while controlling the KL divergence between consecutive policies (Shani et al., 2020; Cai et al., 2020; Zhong and Zhang, 2023), sharing the principle of limiting policy changes with TRPO (Schulman et al., 2015) and with PPO and GRPO, which are used in LLM post-training (Schulman et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024). We study NPG to shed light on the training dynamics of RL algorithms used in modern LLM post-training.

Proposition 3.1.

Under the softmax parameterization, the exact and sampled NPG directions are given by:

ℱ†(θ)∇J(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}(\theta)\nabla J(\theta) =(𝐈−𝟏𝟏⊤|𝒴|)[𝐫−γ(θ−logπref(⋅∣x))],\displaystyle=\Big(\mathbf{I}-\frac{\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\Big)\left[\mathbf{r}-\gamma(\theta-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x))\right], (3.4)
ℱ†​(θ^)​∇J^​(θ^)\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}(\widehat{\theta})\widehat{\nabla J}(\widehat{\theta}) =(𝐈−𝟏𝟏⊤|𝒴|)[1B∑b=1Br⁡(x,yb)πθ^​(yb∣x)𝐞yb−γ(θ^−logπref(⋅∣x))].\displaystyle=\Big(\mathbf{I}-\frac{\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\Big)\Big[\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\frac{r(x,y_{b})}{\pi_{\widehat{\theta}}(y_{b}\mid x)}\mathbf{e}_{y_{b}}-\gamma(\widehat{\theta}-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x))\Big]. (3.5)

Here BB denotes the batch size used to estimate the policy gradient, and y1,…,yB∼iidπθ^(⋅∣x)y_{1},\ldots,y_{B}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}\pi_{\widehat{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x) are the sampled responses. Let 𝐈\mathbf{I} be the identity matrix, 𝟏\mathbf{1} the all-ones vector, and 𝐞y\mathbf{e}_{y} the one-hot vector corresponding to response yy.

Exponential Moving Average (EMA) momentum. In classical optimization, Polyak’s heavy-ball momentum can accelerate convergence under suitable curvature and parameter conditions (Polyak, 1964), and global convergence guarantees are available for smooth convex objectives (Ghadimi et al., 2015). EMA is its normalized form and is widely used in modern LLM training optimizers, such as Adam and AdamW (Kingma and Ba, 2015; Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019). EMA maintains a first-moment momentum mtm_{t}, where the EMA coefficient β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) controls the contribution of the current gradient to the parameter update. With exact gradients, the NPG update with EMA is given by

mt+1=βmt+(1−β)ℱ†(θtβ)∇J(θtβ),θt+1β=θtβ+ηmt+11−βt+1.m_{t+1}=\beta m_{t}+(1-\beta)\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}(\theta_{t}^{\beta})\nabla J(\theta_{t}^{\beta}),\qquad\theta_{t+1}^{\beta}=\theta_{t}^{\beta}+\eta\frac{m_{t+1}}{1-\beta^{t+1}}. (3.6)

The initial condition is m0=0m_{0}=0 and θtβ\theta_{t}^{\beta} denotes the parameter vector updated by EMA with coefficient β\beta at iteration tt. In the stochastic setting, we replace ∇J​(⋅)\nabla J(\cdot) with its unbiased estimator and denote the corresponding parameter vector by θ^tβ\widehat{\theta}^{\beta}_{t}.

Without EMA, the current natural gradient is applied in full to the current parameter update. With EMA, a gradient’s contribution is spread across the current and subsequent updates, while each update uses a weighted sum of the current and past natural gradients. Thus, EMA can be viewed as a temporal reallocation of gradient contributions to parameter updates. To isolate this reallocation from changes in the total gradient weight, we normalize mtm_{t} by 1−βt1-\beta^{t} for t≥1t\geq 1 before using it to update the parameters. This makes the gradient weights in each update sum to one, following the first-moment bias correction used in Adam and AdamW.

Let ωβ​(t,t′)\omega_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime}) denote the weight of the gradient at time t′t^{\prime} in the update at time tt, under EMA with coefficient β\beta. For β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), (3.6) can be rewritten as

θt+1β=θtβ+η∑t′=0tωβ(t,t′)ℱ†(θt′β)∇J(θt′β),ωβ(t,t′)=(1−β)​βt−t′1−βt+1.\displaystyle\theta_{t+1}^{\beta}=\theta_{t}^{\beta}+\eta\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{t}\omega_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime})\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}(\theta_{t^{\prime}}^{\beta})\nabla J(\theta_{t^{\prime}}^{\beta}),\qquad\omega_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime})=\frac{(1-\beta)\beta^{t-t^{\prime}}}{1-\beta^{t+1}}. (3.7)

The stochastic update uses the same weights. In particular, we define ω0​(t,t′)=0\omega_{0}(t,t^{\prime})=0 for all t′≠tt^{\prime}\neq t and ω0​(t,t)=1\omega_{0}(t,t)=1, which recovers the standard NPG update without EMA. For consistency, we use the same notation with β=0\beta=0 to denote the corresponding quantities for vanilla NPG without EMA.

4 Deterministic case: acceleration with exact gradients

In this section, we consider deterministic optimization with exact policy gradients, where the natural-gradient direction is given by (3.4). Maximizing JJ in (3.1) yields the unique optimal policy π⋆​(y∣x)∝πref​(y∣x)​exp⁡(r⁡(x,y)/γ)\pi^{\star}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp(r(x,y)/\gamma). For an arbitrary initial parameter θ0\theta_{0}, define

θ⋆:=logπref(⋅∣x)+𝐫γ+𝟏⊤[θ0−logπref(⋅∣x)−𝐫/γ]𝟏|𝒴|,\displaystyle\theta^{\star}:=\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)+\frac{\mathbf{r}}{\gamma}+\frac{\mathbf{1}^{\top}\left[\theta_{0}-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)-\mathbf{r}/\gamma\right]\mathbf{1}}{|\mathcal{Y}|}, (4.1)

which is one of the maximizers of JJ and induces π⋆\pi^{\star}. Here 𝐫\mathbf{r} is the reward vector and |𝒴||\mathcal{Y}| is the number of possible responses. We compare the exact NPG iterates obtained with EMA coefficient β\beta against those obtained without EMA (β=0\beta=0). Both runs are initialized at θ0\theta_{0} with m0=0m_{0}=0 and use the same learning rate η\eta and number of updates TT.

Following the update in (3.6), we recursively define a family of functions {ft:[0,1)→ℝ}t≥0\{f_{t}:[0,1)\to\mathbb{R}\}_{t\geq 0} by f0​(β)=1f_{0}(\beta)=1 and ft+1​(β)=ft​(β)−η​γ​∑t′=0tωβ​(t,t′)​ft′​(β)f_{t+1}(\beta)=f_{t}(\beta)-\eta\gamma\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{t}\omega_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime})f_{t^{\prime}}(\beta) for t≥0t\geq 0. In particular, for vanilla NPG, ft​(0)=(1−η​γ)tf_{t}(0)=(1-\eta\gamma)^{t}. The following lemma shows that these functions characterize the natural policy gradient and the parameter error at each iteration.

Lemma 4.1 (Exact dynamics).

The exact NPG iterates in (3.6) satisfy, for every t≥0t\geq 0,

ℱ†(θtβ)∇J(θtβ)=ft(β)ℱ†(θ0)∇J(θ0),θtβ−θ⋆=ft(β)(θ0−θ⋆).\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}(\theta_{t}^{\beta})\nabla J(\theta_{t}^{\beta})=f_{t}(\beta)\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}(\theta_{0})\nabla J(\theta_{0}),\qquad\theta_{t}^{\beta}-\theta^{\star}=f_{t}(\beta)(\theta_{0}-\theta^{\star}). (4.2)

The proof is in Appendix B. Lemma 4.1 shows that the exact natural gradients at all iterations are collinear and that the parameter error θtβ−θ⋆\theta_{t}^{\beta}-\theta^{\star} remains a scalar multiple of θ0−θ⋆\theta_{0}-\theta^{\star}. As long as ft′​(β)>0f_{t^{\prime}}(\beta)>0 for all 0≤t′≤t0\leq t^{\prime}\leq t, the iterates up to time tt do not overshoot θ⋆\theta^{\star}. Over these iterations, the iterates θt′β\theta_{t^{\prime}}^{\beta} approach θ⋆\theta^{\star}, so the natural gradients point in the same direction and decrease in magnitude. EMA averages the current natural gradient with earlier, larger ones, which can accelerate optimization. The following theorem gives a sufficient range that prevents overshoot and establishes a strict benefit from increasing β\beta. The proof is in Appendix B.

Theorem 4.2 (Strict acceleration from momentum).

Assume 0<η​γ<10<\eta\gamma<1 and T≥2T\geq 2. For any β1,β2\beta_{1},\beta_{2} in the range [0,((1−η​γ)/(1+η​γ))2][0,((1-\eta\gamma)/(1+\eta\gamma))^{2}] with β1<β2\beta_{1}<\beta_{2}, we have J⁡(θTβ2)>J⁡(θTβ1)J(\theta_{T}^{\beta_{2}})>J(\theta_{T}^{\beta_{1}}). In particular, every positive β\beta in this range satisfies J⁡(θTβ)>J⁡(θT0)J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})>J(\theta_{T}^{0}).

Thus, within the stated range, EMA accelerates deterministic optimization at the same learning rate and update count through a temporal reallocation of natural gradients. This raises two questions: Why can a strictly positive exact-gradient benefit fail to yield a reliable improvement in sampled training? How can this benefit be reliably realized and exploited in sampled training?

5 Stochastic case: sampling fluctuations and expected gain

We now study the stochastic setting, where natural gradients are estimated from sampled responses, introducing noise into the updates. To analyze training dynamics at small learning rates, we fix the problem, the batch size B≥1B\geq 1, and the optimization time τ=η​T>0\tau=\eta T>0, and let η=τ/T→0\eta=\tau/T\to 0. We compare J⁡(θ^Tβ)J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta}) and J⁡(θ^T0)J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0}) obtained with and without EMA. The two runs share the same settings, including the initial parameter θ0\theta_{0}, zero initial momentum, learning rate η\eta, batch size BB, and update count TT, while using independent samples even when β=0\beta=0. Expectations and variances are over training randomness. The objective JJ is evaluated exactly.

By Proposition 3.1, the sampled natural-gradient direction is conditionally unbiased. Taking expectations in the EMA updates then gives 𝔼⁡[θ^tβ]=θtβ\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}]=\theta_{t}^{\beta}. To characterize the expected objective, we must also account for sampling fluctuations. Let ΣTβ\Sigma_{T}^{\beta} denote a covariance coefficient characterizing the accumulated sampling noise along the exact trajectory θtβ\theta_{t}^{\beta}. It is a nonnegative weighted sum of noise covariance matrices evaluated along this trajectory, where the noise comes from estimating the reward vector 𝐫\mathbf{r} using a single sampled response. This coefficient is a deterministic positive semidefinite matrix, independent of the realized samples. Its precise definition is given in Appendix C. Using this coefficient, the following lemma expresses the expected objective difference as the exact difference plus a sampling correction.

Lemma 5.1 (Expected objective difference).

Fix B≥1B\geq 1 and τ>0\tau>0. For any β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1), as η=τ/T→0\eta=\tau/T\to 0, the expected objective difference satisfies

𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]=J⁡(θTβ)−J⁡(θT0)+η2​B​tr​[∇2J​(θTβ)​ΣTβ−∇2J​(θT0)​ΣT0]+O⁡((η/B)3/2).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})\right]=J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})-J(\theta_{T}^{0})+\frac{\eta}{2B}\operatorname{tr}\left[\nabla^{2}J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}-\nabla^{2}J(\theta_{T}^{0})\Sigma_{T}^{0}\right]+O((\eta/B)^{3/2}). (5.1)

The remainder is uniform in β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1), and supβ∈[0,1)‖ΣTβ‖op\sup_{\beta\in[0,1)}\|\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}\|_{\mathrm{op}} is bounded independently of η\eta.

Establishing the expansion in Lemma 5.1 requires controlling sampling fluctuations throughout training. This is challenging because the sampled natural-gradient direction weights rewards by inverse sampling probabilities: a sampled response with positive reward and very small probability can produce a large noise term. To control this noise, we construct an auxiliary parameter update process whose distance from the exact iterates is bounded. Since the exact trajectory is bounded, the sampling probabilities in this auxiliary process stay bounded away from zero, and its sampling noise is bounded. During training, the probability that the auxiliary process and the original sampled process differ is sufficiently small. Therefore, we can characterize the expected objective difference using the auxiliary process. A proof sketch follows and Appendix C gives the full proof.

Proof sketch. Let εtβ\varepsilon_{t}^{\beta} denote the estimation noise in the sampled natural gradient at θ^tβ\widehat{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}. We construct an auxiliary process driven by the same noise sequence, initialized at θ~0β=θ0\widetilde{\theta}_{0}^{\beta}=\theta_{0} and defined by

ε~tβ=𝟏{maxt′≤t∥θ~t′β−θt′β∥∞≤1}εtβ,θ~t+1β=θ~tβ+η∑t′=0tωβ(t,t′)[ℱ†(θ~t′β)∇J(θ~t′β)+ε~t′β].\displaystyle\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{t}^{\beta}=\mathbf{1}\Big\{\max_{t^{\prime}\leq t}\|\widetilde{\theta}_{t^{\prime}}^{\beta}-\theta_{t^{\prime}}^{\beta}\|_{\infty}\leq 1\Big\}\varepsilon_{t}^{\beta},\quad\widetilde{\theta}_{t+1}^{\beta}=\widetilde{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}+\eta\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{t}\omega_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime})\left[\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}(\widetilde{\theta}_{t^{\prime}}^{\beta})\nabla J(\widetilde{\theta}_{t^{\prime}}^{\beta})+\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{t^{\prime}}^{\beta}\right].

The two processes coincide through the first exit from the unit neighborhood of the exact path. After this exit, the exact direction and EMA memory continue to evolve, while no further sampling noise enters the auxiliary process. The construction gives maxt≤T⁡‖θ~tβ−θtβ‖∞=O⁡(1)\max_{t\leq T}\|\widetilde{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}-\theta_{t}^{\beta}\|_{\infty}=O(1) for every sample path. Since the exact trajectory is bounded, this implies inft≤T,y∈𝒴πθ~tβ​(y∣x)=Ω⁡(1)\inf_{t\leq T,y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\widetilde{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}}(y\mid x)=\Omega(1) and maxt<T⁡‖ε~tβ‖∞=O⁡(1)\max_{t<T}\|\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{t}^{\beta}\|_{\infty}=O(1). These bounds allow us to estimate the covariance and third moment of the auxiliary parameter fluctuations. A second-order Taylor expansion, together with a comparison of the noise covariances along the auxiliary and exact paths, then yields

𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ~Tβ)]=J⁡(θTβ)+η2​B​tr⁡[∇2J​(θTβ)​ΣTβ]+O⁡((η/B)3/2).\mathbb{E}[J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})]=J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})+\frac{\eta}{2B}\operatorname{tr}\left[\nabla^{2}J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}\right]+O((\eta/B)^{3/2}).

For each fixed update and coordinate, the weighted noise contributions have zero conditional mean, so their partial sums form a martingale. Using a concentration bound and a union bound, we show that the probability of path separation is sufficiently small, uniformly in β\beta. Since JJ is bounded, we obtain

|𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)]−𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ~Tβ)]|\displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})]-\mathbb{E}[J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})]\right| ≤2supθ|J(θ)|ℙ(∃t≤T:θ^tβ≠θ~tβ)=o((η/B)3/2).\displaystyle\leq 2\sup_{\theta}|J(\theta)|\,\mathbb{P}(\exists\,t\leq T:\widehat{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}\neq\widetilde{\theta}_{t}^{\beta})=o((\eta/B)^{3/2}).

Combining these estimates and subtracting the expansions for β\beta and 00 proves Lemma 5.1.

Applying the same analysis to J2J^{2} also allows us to quantify the fluctuations in the objective difference through its variance.

Proposition 5.2 (Variance of the objective difference).

Under the conditions of Lemma 5.1, the independent runs satisfy the following expansion uniformly in β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1):

Var[J(θ^Tβ)−J(θ^T0)]=ηB[∇J(θTβ)⊤ΣTβ∇J(θTβ)+∇J(θT0)⊤ΣT0∇J(θT0)]+O((η/B)3/2).\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}\left[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})\right]=\frac{\eta}{B}\left[\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})^{\top}\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})+\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{0})^{\top}\Sigma_{T}^{0}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{0})\right]+O((\eta/B)^{3/2}). (5.2)

Under the nondegeneracy condition, specifically, lim infη→0∇J(θT0)⊤ΣT0∇J(θT0)>0\liminf_{\eta\to 0}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{0})^{\top}\Sigma_{T}^{0}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{0})>0, uniformly over β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1), we have

Var⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]=Θ⁡(η/B).\operatorname{Var}\big[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})\big]=\Theta(\eta/B). (5.3)

The proof is in Appendix D. Proposition 5.2 shows that the variance of the objective difference remains of order η/B\eta/B regardless of the EMA coefficient. Lemma 5.1 shows that the expected difference is characterized by the exact objective difference. Thus, when the exact gain is small relative to the standard-deviation scale η/B\sqrt{\eta/B}, training fluctuations make a consistent benefit from EMA difficult to observe.

The critical metric is ρ=η/(1−β).\rho=\eta/(1-\beta). Intuitively, EMA averages natural gradients over an effective memory window of 1/(1−β)1/(1-\beta) steps. Since each exact update moves the parameters by O⁡(η)O(\eta), the averaged gradients span a parameter-displacement scale of O⁡(η/(1−β))O(\eta/(1-\beta)), which controls their difference from the current gradient. When this ratio is small, gradients vary little within the window, so EMA behaves similarly to the update without momentum and the difference vanishes. The next two subsections quantify the cases of a vanishing or fixed positive ratio.

5.1 A fixed EMA coefficient gives a vanishing expected gain

Theorem 5.3 (Fixed EMA coefficient).

Fix β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), B≥1B\geq 1, τ>0\tau>0, and suppose that the nondegeneracy condition in Proposition 5.2 holds. As η=τ/T→0\eta=\tau/T\to 0, the expected objective gain satisfies

𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]=C⁡(τ,γ)​η​β1−β+O⁡(η3/2),\mathbb{E}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]=C(\tau,\gamma)\frac{\eta\beta}{1-\beta}+O(\eta^{3/2}), (5.4)

where C⁡(τ,γ)C(\tau,\gamma) is a positive constant depending only on τ\tau, γ\gamma, and the fixed problem. It is independent of β\beta. The probability that EMA yields a higher objective value satisfies

limη→0ℙ⁡(J⁡(θ^Tβ)>J⁡(θ^T0))=1/2.\lim_{\eta\to 0}\mathbb{P}\big(J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})>J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})\big)=1/2. (5.5)

The proof is in Appendix E. Theorem 5.3 shows that fixed β\beta gives a positive expected gain for sufficiently small η\eta, but the gain is only of order η\eta, which matches the variance order in Proposition 5.2 with fixed batch size. Sampling fluctuations therefore overwhelm the gain, making the two algorithms difficult to distinguish in individual runs. This offers a possible explanation for the limited benefits of momentum reported in prior RLVR experiments (Mukherjee et al., 2026).

5.2 Scaling the EMA coefficient with the learning rate

Beyond Theorem 5.3, we further show that η/(1−β)→0\eta/(1-\beta)\to 0 forces the expected gain to vanish, even when β\beta depends on η\eta. The full proof is given in Appendix F. To satisfy the sufficient condition for avoiding overshoot in Theorem 4.2, this ratio must remain bounded. Thus, a nonvanishing expected gain requires η/(1−β)=Θ⁡(1)\eta/(1-\beta)=\Theta(1). For simplicity, we set β\beta so that η/(1−β)=ρ\eta/(1-\beta)=\rho, where ρ>η\rho>\eta is a positive constant. In Appendix G, we prove that ρ∈(0,1/(4​γ)]\rho\in(0,1/(4\gamma)] ensures the sufficient condition in Theorem 4.2. The following theorem compares the objective values of two independent runs with and without EMA in this setting.

Theorem 5.4 (EMA coefficient scaling with the learning rate).

Fix B≥1B\geq 1, τ>0\tau>0, and 0<ρ≤1/(4​γ)0<\rho\leq 1/(4\gamma), and suppose that the nondegeneracy condition in Proposition 5.2 holds. Set β=1−η/ρ\beta=1-\eta/\rho. As η=τ/T→0\eta=\tau/T\to 0, the expected objective gain satisfies

𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]=C⁡(τ,γ,ρ)​β​ρ+O⁡(η),\mathbb{E}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]=C(\tau,\gamma,\rho)\beta\rho+O(\eta), (5.6)

where C⁡(τ,γ,ρ)C(\tau,\gamma,\rho) is a positive constant depending only on τ\tau, γ\gamma, ρ\rho, and the fixed problem. It is independent of η\eta and β\beta. The probability that EMA yields a higher objective value satisfies

ℙ⁡(J⁡(θ^Tβ)>J⁡(θ^T0))=1−O⁡(η/B).\mathbb{P}\big(J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})>J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})\big)=1-O(\eta/B). (5.7)

The proof is in Appendix G. When ρ=η/(1−β)\rho=\eta/(1-\beta) is held at a fixed positive value in the safe regime, Theorem 5.4 gives a nonvanishing expected gain, while Proposition 5.2 shows that the standard deviation of the objective difference is of order η/B\sqrt{\eta/B}. As η→0\eta\to 0, the expected gain therefore dominates sampling fluctuations, and EMA’s advantage becomes consistently observable in the stochastic case. These findings suggest that choosing β\beta substantially above the conventional fixed value can yield greater benefits in practice.

5.3 Reducing variability across runs with EMA

We next investigate whether EMA can help reduce variability across runs while achieving comparable expected performance under the same training budget. A smaller learning rate can reduce sampling fluctuations, but it may also slow optimization over a given number of updates. The deterministic acceleration established in Section 4 suggests that increasing the EMA coefficient may compensate for this slower progress. We compare two independent EMA runs with settings (η1,β1)(\eta_{1},\beta_{1}) and (η2,β2)(\eta_{2},\beta_{2}), using the same initialization, batch size BB, and update count TT. We write θT(i)\theta_{T}^{(i)} and θ^T(i)\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{(i)} for the parameters obtained with exact and sampled gradients, respectively, under setting i=1,2i=1,2.

Theorem 5.5 (Comparable expected performance with lower variance).

Fix B>1B>1 and τ>0\tau>0. For any (η1,β1)(\eta_{1},\beta_{1}) with η1=τ/T\eta_{1}=\tau/T and T≥2T\geq 2, and any ρ2\rho_{2} satisfying 0<ρ1=η1/(1−β1)<ρ2≤1/(4​γ)0<\rho_{1}=\eta_{1}/(1-\beta_{1})<\rho_{2}\leq 1/(4\gamma), there exist 0<η2<η10<\eta_{2}<\eta_{1} and β1<β2<1\beta_{1}<\beta_{2}<1 such that η2/(1−β2)=ρ2\eta_{2}/(1-\beta_{2})=\rho_{2} and θT(2)=θT(1)\theta_{T}^{(2)}=\theta_{T}^{(1)}. As η1→0\eta_{1}\to 0 with ρ1,ρ2\rho_{1},\rho_{2} fixed, the expected objective difference and the limiting variance ratio satisfy

𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ^T(2))−J⁡(θ^T(1))]=O⁡(η1/B),limτ→∞limη1→0Var⁡[J⁡(θ^T(2))]Var⁡[J⁡(θ^T(1))]=1+1−4​γ​ρ21+1−4​γ​ρ1<1.\mathbb{E}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{(2)})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{(1)})]=O(\eta_{1}/B),\qquad\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\lim_{\eta_{1}\to 0}\frac{\operatorname{Var}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{(2)})]}{\operatorname{Var}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{(1)})]}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1-4\gamma\rho_{2}}}{1+\sqrt{1-4\gamma\rho_{1}}}<1. (5.8)

The proof is in Appendix H. Increasing the EMA coefficient compensates for the smaller learning rate by matching the parameters obtained with exact gradients after the same number of updates. With sampled gradients, the expected objective values differ by O⁡(η1/B)O(\eta_{1}/B), while the variance ratio converges to a constant below one in the stated asymptotic regime. Thus, EMA can help reduce variability across runs while achieving comparable expected performance under the same update count TT and sample budget B​TBT.

6 Experiments

We use numerical bandit experiments to quantitatively validate the predictions of Proposition 5.2 and Theorems 5.3 and 5.4. Then we turn to RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base to test our theoretical predictions in a practical LLM post-training setting. Finally, we apply our principle of increasing the EMA coefficient to Qwen2.5-32B to assess its applicability as model size increases.

6.1 Validating theoretical predictions in bandits

Setup. We consider a 10-arm bandit in which 33 arms have reward 11 and the remaining 77 have reward 00. The reference policy is set equal to the initial policy, with KL penalty coefficient γ=1\gamma=1, batch size B=1B=1, and optimization time τ=1\tau=1. Training uses T=32,64,…,4096T=32,64,\ldots,4096 updates with learning rate η=1/T\eta=1/T. We compare sampled NPG with fixed β=0.9\beta=0.9 or scaled β=1−4​η\beta=1-4\eta against the no-EMA baseline. Each configuration uses 50,00050{,}000 independent training replicates, with JJ evaluated exactly after training, to estimate the expectation and standard deviation of the objective gap J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0}) and the probability of outperforming an independent no-EMA run. To measure the gain relative to these fluctuations, we compare SNR of the objective gap, defined as SNR:=|𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]|/Std⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]\operatorname{SNR}:=|\mathbb{E}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]|/\operatorname{Std}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]. Both uniform and random policy initializations are considered. Additional experiments with different reward configurations are provided in Appendix I.1.

Results. As the learning rate η\eta decreases, Figure 1 shows that the standard deviation scales as η\sqrt{\eta} for small η\eta under both momentum schedules, as predicted by Proposition 5.2. With fixed β=0.9\beta=0.9, the mean gain remains positive for small η\eta but scales as η\eta, decreasing faster than the standard deviation. With scaled β=1−4​η\beta=1-4\eta, it approaches a positive constant, consistent with Theorems 5.3 and 5.4. These trends hold under both uniform and random initialization. At η=1/4096\eta=1/4096, fixed β\beta gives SNRs of 0.0453 and 0.0406 under uniform and random initialization, respectively, while scaled β\beta gives 3.7647 and 3.3982. (More details are reported in Table 1.) The probability of EMA outperforming an independent no-EMA run approaches 1/21/2 with fixed β\beta and 11 with scaled β\beta.

6.2 Practical LLM post-training

Setup. We conduct RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), using the DAPO-17k-processed dataset with 1,0001{,}000 problems held out for validation. We vary β\beta in SGD with bias-corrected EMA and, to support our claim in a more practical setting, also study AdamW by varying β1\beta_{1} while fixing β2=0.999\beta_{2}=0.999. Setting β=0\beta=0 recovers vanilla SGD, while β1=0\beta_{1}=0 gives an RMSProp-style optimizer. All configurations share the same data and evaluation protocol. We use three training generation seeds per configuration to show that our findings are consistent. Details of the experimental setup are provided in Appendix I.2.

Benefits of larger momentum coefficients. For SGD with EMA, we compare β∈{0,0.9,0.9992}\beta\in\{0,0.9,0.9992\} at η=2×10−2\eta=2\times 10^{-2} (Figure 2(a)). We choose β=0.9992\beta=0.9992 so that η/(1−β)\eta/(1-\beta) equals the upper bound 1/(4​γ)1/(4\gamma) suggested by Theorem 5.4. For AdamW, we compare β1∈{0,0.9,1−10−6}\beta_{1}\in\{0,0.9,1-10^{-6}\} at η=1×10−6\eta=1\times 10^{-6} (Figure 2(b)). For both optimizers, the tuned larger momentum coefficient substantially improves validation performance over the conventional value of 0.90.9 and the baseline without first-moment momentum. These results support our claim that choosing momentum coefficients substantially above the conventional value of 0.90.9 can yield greater benefits in practical RLVR training.

More stable training without hurting performance. For SGD with EMA, we compare (η,β)=(1×10−2,0.9996)(\eta,\beta)=(1\times 10^{-2},0.9996) with (2×10−2,0.9)(2\times 10^{-2},0.9) and include (1×10−2,0.9)(1\times 10^{-2},0.9) as a baseline (Figure 2(c)). Here, β=0.9996\beta=0.9996 is chosen to satisfy η/(1−β)=1/(4​γ)\eta/(1-\beta)=1/(4\gamma). For AdamW, we compare (η,β1)=(5×10−7,1−10−6)(\eta,\beta_{1})=(5\times 10^{-7},1-10^{-6}) with (1×10−6,0.9)(1\times 10^{-6},0.9) and include (5×10−7,0.9)(5\times 10^{-7},0.9) as a baseline (Figure 2(d)). Under the same update and sample budgets, using a larger momentum coefficient at the smaller learning rate preserves the low variability in final validation accuracy across seeds while achieving slightly better performance than runs using the larger learning rate with conventional momentum. These results show that pairing a larger momentum coefficient with a smaller learning rate makes training more stable while maintaining or even slightly improving performance.

6.3 Extending to a larger model

We apply the same GRPO setup to Qwen2.5-32B and increase the momentum coefficient in AdamW from 0.90.9 to 1−10−91-10^{-9}, using a learning rate of 2×10−62\times 10^{-6}. Simply increasing the momentum coefficient β1\beta_{1} substantially improves validation performance. At step 150150, the conventional β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9 achieves a mean accuracy of 44.3%44.3\%, similar to 44.2%44.2\% for the baseline without first-moment momentum, whereas β1=1−10−9\beta_{1}=1-10^{-9} reaches 46.1%46.1\%, nearly 2 percentage points higher than the conventional setting. Results are shown in Figure 3.

7 Conclusion

In this work, we explain why momentum’s benefit can be obscured by sampling noise and derive a principle for recovering and exploiting it. We develop a theoretical model and prove that EMA strictly improves the objective value under exact gradients within a range that prevents overshoot. With sampled gradients, fixing β\beta as η\eta decreases makes the expected gain vanish faster than sampling fluctuations, whereas suitably increasing β\beta within the safe regime produces a consistent improvement. GRPO experiments on LLMs confirm the practical benefits of larger momentum coefficients. These findings suggest using coefficients substantially above the conventional β=0.9\beta=0.9 to better exploit the first-moment information already maintained by the optimizer.

Appendix A Proof of Proposition 3.1

Proof.

We first identify the softmax geometry and then derive the exact and sampled natural gradients.

Policy Jacobian and Fisher matrix. Differentiating the softmax parameterization, we have

∂πθ​(y∣x)∂θ⁡(x,y′)=πθ(y∣x)(𝟏{y=y′}−πθ(y′∣x)),∇logπθ(y∣x)=𝐞y−πθ(⋅∣x),\frac{\partial\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{\partial\theta(x,y^{\prime})}=\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\big(\mathbf{1}_{\{y=y^{\prime}\}}-\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)\big),\quad\nabla\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)=\mathbf{e}_{y}-\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x), (A.1)

where 𝐞y\mathbf{e}_{y} is the one-hot vector corresponding to y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. Substituting the second identity into the definition of the Fisher information matrix in (3.2) and comparing with the first gives

ℱ(θ)=diag(πθ(⋅∣x))−πθ(⋅∣x)πθ(⋅∣x)⊤=∂πθ(⋅∣x)∂θ⊤.\mathcal{F}(\theta)=\operatorname{diag}\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\big)-\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)^{\top}=\frac{\partial\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}{\partial\theta^{\top}}. (A.2)

Since the policy has full support, ℱ⁡(θ)\mathcal{F}(\theta) is positive semidefinite with null space span⁡{𝟏}\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{1}\}. Hence ℱ†​(θ)​ℱ​(θ)=𝐈−𝟏𝟏⊤/|𝒴|\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}(\theta)\mathcal{F}(\theta)=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}/|\mathcal{Y}|.

Exact and sampled natural gradients. By the chain rule, differentiating (3.1) gives

∇J​(θ)\displaystyle\nabla J(\theta) =(∂πθ(⋅∣x)∂θ⊤)⊤𝐫−γ∑y∈𝒴(logπθ​(y∣x)πref​(y∣x)+1)∇πθ(y∣x)\displaystyle=\Big(\frac{\partial\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}{\partial\theta^{\top}}\Big)^{\top}\mathbf{r}-\gamma\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\Big(\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)}+1\Big)\nabla\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)
=ℱ(θ)[𝐫−γ(logπθ(⋅∣x)−logπref(⋅∣x)+𝟏)]\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}(\theta)\left[\mathbf{r}-\gamma\left(\log\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)+\mathbf{1}\right)\right]
=ℱ(θ)[𝐫−γ(θ−logπref(⋅∣x))].\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}(\theta)\left[\mathbf{r}-\gamma\big(\theta-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\big)\right]. (A.3)

The second equality follows from (A.2). The last uses logπθ(⋅∣x)=θ−log(∑y∈𝒴exp(θ(x,y)))𝟏\log\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)=\theta-\log(\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\exp(\theta(x,y)))\mathbf{1} and ℱ⁡(θ)​𝟏=0\mathcal{F}(\theta)\mathbf{1}=0. For the sampled gradient, the KL term is evaluated exactly, so

∇J^​(θ^)\displaystyle\widehat{\nabla J}(\widehat{\theta}) =1B∑b=1Br(x,yb)∇logπθ^(yb∣x)−γ∇KL(πθ^(⋅∣x)∥πref(⋅∣x))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}r(x,y_{b})\nabla\log\pi_{\widehat{\theta}}(y_{b}\mid x)-\gamma\nabla\operatorname{KL}\big(\pi_{\widehat{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x)\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\big)
=ℱ(θ^)[1B∑b=1Br⁡(x,yb)πθ^​(yb∣x)𝐞yb−γ(θ^−logπref(⋅∣x))].\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}(\widehat{\theta})\Big[\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\frac{r(x,y_{b})}{\pi_{\widehat{\theta}}(y_{b}\mid x)}\mathbf{e}_{y_{b}}-\gamma\big(\widehat{\theta}-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\big)\Big]. (A.4)

The second equality uses ℱ(θ^)𝐞yb/πθ^(yb∣x)=𝐞yb−πθ^(⋅∣x)\mathcal{F}(\widehat{\theta})\mathbf{e}_{y_{b}}/\pi_{\widehat{\theta}}(y_{b}\mid x)=\mathbf{e}_{y_{b}}-\pi_{\widehat{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x). Premultiplying (A.3) and (A.4) by the corresponding Fisher pseudoinverse proves (3.4) and (3.5). ∎

Optimality of θ⋆\theta^{\star}. The definition of θ⋆\theta^{\star} gives πθ⋆​(y∣x)∝πref​(y∣x)​er⁡(x,y)/γ\pi_{\theta^{\star}}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)e^{r(x,y)/\gamma}. Substituting this identity into (3.1), we obtain

Appendix C Proof of Lemma 5.1

Proof.

We first construct an auxiliary process with bounded noise and control its exit probability and moments. We then use these estimates to derive the objective expansion for the auxiliary process and transfer it to the original process.

Sampling noise and its propagation. Let yt,bβy_{t,b}^{\beta} be the bb-th response at update tt. Conditional on the sample history, the batch consists of independent responses from πθ^tβ(⋅∣x)\pi_{\widehat{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}}(\cdot\mid x). Let εt,bβ\varepsilon_{t,b}^{\beta} denote the estimation noise from the bb-th response at update tt. Then we have

εt,bβ=(𝐈−𝟏𝟏⊤|𝒴|)​[r⁡(x,yt,bβ)πθ^tβ​(yt,bβ∣x)​𝐞yt,bβ−𝐫],εtβ=1B​∑b=1Bεt,bβ.\varepsilon_{t,b}^{\beta}=\left(\mathbf{I}-\frac{\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\right)\left[\frac{r(x,y_{t,b}^{\beta})}{\pi_{\widehat{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}}(y_{t,b}^{\beta}\mid x)}\mathbf{e}_{y_{t,b}^{\beta}}-\mathbf{r}\right],\qquad\varepsilon_{t}^{\beta}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\varepsilon_{t,b}^{\beta}. (C.1)

Since the sampled directions have zero coordinate sum (3.5) and the initial momentum is zero, the updates preserve 𝟏⊤​θ^tβ=𝟏⊤​θ0=𝟏⊤​θ⋆\mathbf{1}^{\top}\widehat{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}=\mathbf{1}^{\top}\theta_{0}=\mathbf{1}^{\top}\theta^{\star}. Therefore, the sampled direction at update tt in Proposition 3.1 can be written as γ⁡(θ⋆−θ^tβ)+εtβ\gamma(\theta^{\star}-\widehat{\theta}_{t}^{\beta})+\varepsilon_{t}^{\beta}. Each εt,bβ\varepsilon_{t,b}^{\beta} has conditional mean zero, so the expected direction is γ⁡(θ⋆−𝔼⁡[θ^tβ])\gamma(\theta^{\star}-\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}]). Thus, after taking expectations, the sampled EMA updates obey the same recurrence as the exact updates. With the same initial parameter and zero initial momentum, this gives 𝔼⁡[θ^tβ]=θtβ\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}]=\theta_{t}^{\beta} by induction.

Let Ψβ​(t,t′)\Psi_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime}) denote the weight of the noise εt′β\varepsilon_{t^{\prime}}^{\beta} in the difference between the sampled and exact parameters, so that θ^tβ−θtβ=∑t′=0t−1Ψβ​(t,t′)​εt′β.\widehat{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}-\theta_{t}^{\beta}=\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{t-1}\Psi_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime})\varepsilon_{t^{\prime}}^{\beta}. Subtracting the exact EMA update from the sampled EMA update gives

θ^t+1β−θt+1β=θ^tβ−θtβ+η​∑t′=0tωβ​(t,t′)​[−γ⁡(θ^t′β−θt′β)+εt′β].\widehat{\theta}_{t+1}^{\beta}-\theta_{t+1}^{\beta}=\widehat{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}-\theta_{t}^{\beta}+\eta\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{t}\omega_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime})\big[-\gamma(\widehat{\theta}_{t^{\prime}}^{\beta}-\theta_{t^{\prime}}^{\beta})+\varepsilon_{t^{\prime}}^{\beta}\big]. (C.2)

The noise at update t′t^{\prime} first affects the parameter at time t′+1t^{\prime}+1, so Ψβ​(t,t′)=0\Psi_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime})=0 for t≤t′t\leq t^{\prime}. Substituting the noise expansion above into (C.2) gives for all t≥t′t\geq t^{\prime}

Ψβ​(t+1,t′)=Ψβ​(t,t′)−γ​η​∑k=t′tωβ​(t,k)​Ψβ​(k,t′)+η​ωβ​(t,t′).\Psi_{\beta}(t+1,t^{\prime})=\Psi_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime})-\gamma\eta\sum_{k=t^{\prime}}^{t}\omega_{\beta}(t,k)\Psi_{\beta}(k,t^{\prime})+\eta\omega_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime}). (C.3)

ΣTβ=1η​∑t=0T−1Ψβ​(T,t)2​[diag⁡(𝐫πθtβ(⋅∣x))−𝐫𝐫⊤].\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}=\frac{1}{\eta}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\Psi_{\beta}(T,t)^{2}\bigg[\operatorname{diag}\bigg(\frac{\mathbf{r}}{\pi_{\theta_{t}^{\beta}}(\cdot\mid x)}\bigg)-\mathbf{r}\mathbf{r}^{\top}\bigg]. (C.4)

For the bounds below, let ζβ=inf{t≥1:‖θ~tβ−θtβ‖∞>1}\zeta^{\beta}=\inf\{t\geq 1:\|\widetilde{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}-\theta_{t}^{\beta}\|_{\infty}>1\} denote the first exit time, taking ζβ=∞\zeta^{\beta}=\infty if no exit occurs. The two processes agree before exit; afterward, only fresh noise is suppressed. Since the stopping indicator is known before sampling, ε~tβ\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{t}^{\beta} has conditional mean zero, and taking expectations in the auxiliary updates yields 𝔼⁡[θ~tβ]=θtβ\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}]=\theta_{t}^{\beta}.

The bounds on probabilities and noise can be made explicit. Define M=‖θ⋆‖∞+eγ​τ​‖θ0−θ⋆‖∞+1M=\|\theta^{\star}\|_{\infty}+e^{\gamma\tau}\|\theta_{0}-\theta^{\star}\|_{\infty}+1 and L=2​(|𝒴|​e2​M+1)L=2(|\mathcal{Y}|e^{2M}+1). ‖θ~tβ‖∞≤‖θtβ‖∞+1≤‖θ⋆‖∞+|ft​(β)|⋅‖θ0−θ⋆‖∞+1≤M.\|\widetilde{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}\|_{\infty}\leq\|\theta_{t}^{\beta}\|_{\infty}+1\leq\|\theta^{\star}\|_{\infty}+|f_{t}(\beta)|\cdot\|\theta_{0}-\theta^{\star}\|_{\infty}+1\leq M.

Then we have πθ~tβ​(y∣x)≥1/(|𝒴|​exp⁡(2​M))\pi_{\widetilde{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}}(y\mid x)\geq 1/(|\mathcal{Y}|\exp(2M)). According to the definition of the sampling noise in (C.1), on {t<ζβ}\{t<\zeta^{\beta}\}, we have ‖εt,bβ‖∞≤2​(1/πθ~tβ​(yt,bβ∣x)+1)≤2​(|𝒴|​e2​M+1)=L\|\varepsilon_{t,b}^{\beta}\|_{\infty}\leq 2\big(1/\pi_{\widetilde{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}}(y_{t,b}^{\beta}\mid x)+1\big)\leq 2\big(|\mathcal{Y}|e^{2M}+1\big)=L. Applying (C.3) to the auxiliary process and using the second inequality in (C.5) gives for every sample path

maxt≤T⁡‖θ~tβ−θtβ‖∞≤max⁡∑t′=0t−1t≤T⁡|Ψβ​(t,t′)|⋅‖ε~t′β‖∞≤L​τ​eγ​τ.\max_{t\leq T}\|\widetilde{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}-\theta_{t}^{\beta}\|_{\infty}\leq\max_{t\leq T}\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{t-1}|\Psi_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime})|\cdot\|\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{t^{\prime}}^{\beta}\|_{\infty}\leq L\tau e^{\gamma\tau}. Exit probability. We bound the probability that the auxiliary process exits the unit neighborhood of the exact trajectory by time TT. Fix 1≤t≤T1\leq t\leq T. Azuma-Hoeffding’s inequality therefore gives, for every u>0u>0,

ℙ⁡(|(θ~tβ)1−(θtβ)1|>u)≤2​exp⁡[−u22​∑t′=0t−1∑b=1B(L​|Ψβ​(t,t′)|/B)2]≤2​exp⁡[−B​u210​τ​L2​e2​γ​τ​η].\mathbb{P}\big(|(\widetilde{\theta}_{t}^{\beta})_{1}-(\theta_{t}^{\beta})_{1}|>u\big)\leq 2\exp\bigg[-\frac{u^{2}}{2\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{t-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}(L|\Psi_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime})|/B)^{2}}\bigg]\leq 2\exp\bigg[-\frac{Bu^{2}}{10\tau L^{2}e^{2\gamma\tau}\eta}\bigg]. Moment bounds. We next control the second and third moments. For the second moment, we have

maxt≤T⁡𝔼​‖θ~tβ−θtβ‖23≤6|𝒴|∫0∞u2​exp⁡(−B​u210​τ​|𝒴|​L2​e2​γ​τ​η)​𝑑u=O⁡((η/B)3/2).\max_{t\leq T}\mathbb{E}\|\widetilde{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}-\theta_{t}^{\beta}\|_{2}^{3}\leq 6|\mathcal{Y}|\int_{0}^{\infty}u^{2}\exp\bigg(-\frac{Bu^{2}}{10\tau|\mathcal{Y}|L^{2}e^{2\gamma\tau}\eta}\bigg)\,\mathrm{d}u=O((\eta/B)^{3/2}). ≤2|𝒴​|e2​M​5​τ​e2​γ​τ​|𝒴|​L2​η/B+|​𝒴|(e2​M+1)​ℙ​(ζβ≤T)\displaystyle\quad\leq 2|\mathcal{Y}|e^{2M}\sqrt{5\tau e^{2\gamma\tau}|\mathcal{Y}|L^{2}\eta/B}+|\mathcal{Y}|(e^{2M}+1)\mathbb{P}(\zeta^{\beta}\leq T)

We then evaluate the quadratic term in the expansion of J⁡(θ)J(\theta). 𝔼⁡[(θ~Tβ−θTβ)⊤​∇2J​(θTβ)​(θ~Tβ−θTβ)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta}-\theta_{T}^{\beta})^{\top}\nabla^{2}J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta}-\theta_{T}^{\beta})\big]
=1B∑t=0T−1Ψβ(T,t)2𝔼tr[∇2J(θTβ)𝟏{t<ζβ}[diag(𝐫πθ~tβ(⋅∣x))−𝐫𝐫⊤]]\displaystyle\quad=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\Psi_{\beta}(T,t)^{2}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{tr}\bigg[\nabla^{2}J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})\mathbf{1}_{\{t<\zeta^{\beta}\}}\bigg[\operatorname{diag}\bigg(\frac{\mathbf{r}}{\pi_{\widetilde{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}}(\cdot\mid x)}\bigg)-\mathbf{r}\mathbf{r}^{\top}\bigg]\bigg]

Proof.

We bound the residual ft​(β)f_{t}(\beta) and then establish the three noise-response bounds.

where we use ωβ​(t,t′)≥0\omega_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime})\geq 0 and ∑t′=0tωβ​(t,t′)=1\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{t}\omega_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime})=1. Proof of the first inequality in (C.5). Fixing t′t^{\prime} and applying the triangle inequality to (C.3) yields |Ψβ​(t+1,t′)|≤(1+γ​η)​maxt′≤k≤t​|Ψβ​(k,t′)|+η​ωβ​(t,t′).|\Psi_{\beta}(t+1,t^{\prime})|\leq(1+\gamma\eta)\max_{t^{\prime}\leq k\leq t}|\Psi_{\beta}(k,t^{\prime})|+\eta\omega_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime}). =eγ​τ​η​∑k=t′t−1((1−β)​βk−t′+β2​k+1−t′∑ℓ=0kβℓ)\displaystyle=e^{\gamma\tau}\eta\sum_{k=t^{\prime}}^{t-1}\bigg((1-\beta)\beta^{k-t^{\prime}}+\frac{\beta^{2k+1-t^{\prime}}}{\sum_{\ell=0}^{k}\beta^{\ell}}\bigg) (C.19)

Appendix D Proof of Proposition 5.2

Proof.

Apply the expansion proved in Appendix C to J​(θ)2J(\theta)^{2}. Since ∇2(J(θ)2)=2J(θ)∇2J(θ)+2∇J(θ)∇J(θ)⊤\nabla^{2}(J(\theta)^{2})=2J(\theta)\nabla^{2}J(\theta)+2\nabla J(\theta)\nabla J(\theta)^{\top}, it gives

𝔼⁡[J​(θ^Tβ)2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})^{2}] =J(θTβ)2+ηBJ(θTβ)tr[∇2J(θTβ)ΣTβ]+ηB∇J(θTβ)⊤ΣTβ∇J(θTβ)+O((η/B)3/2).\displaystyle=J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})^{2}+\frac{\eta}{B}J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})\operatorname{tr}[\nabla^{2}J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}]+\frac{\eta}{B}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})^{\top}\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})+O((\eta/B)^{3/2}).

Subtracting the square of (C.17) cancels the Hessian term and yields, uniformly in β\beta,

Var[J(θ^Tβ)]=ηB∇J(θTβ)⊤ΣTβ∇J(θTβ)+O((η/B)3/2).\operatorname{Var}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})]=\frac{\eta}{B}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})^{\top}\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})+O((\eta/B)^{3/2}). (D.1)

Independent comparison. The two variances add by independence, proving the expansion in Proposition 5.2. Its two leading quadratic forms are nonnegative and uniformly bounded. Under the stated nondegeneracy condition, the no-EMA term is bounded away from zero as η→0\eta\to 0. Thus, Var⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]=Θ⁡(η/B)\operatorname{Var}\big[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})\big]=\Theta(\eta/B). ∎

Appendix E Proof of Theorem 5.3

Proof.

For fixed β\beta, we first expand the exact objective gain and compare the two sampling corrections in Lemma 5.1 to obtain the expected objective gain. We then combine asymptotic normality with the vanishing mean-to-standard-deviation ratio to derive the limiting winning probability.

Exact objective gain. We first state the required approximation for ft​(β)f_{t}(\beta).

Lemma E.1 (Approximation of ft​(β)f_{t}(\beta)).

For fixed β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1) and τ>0\tau>0, the following approximation for ftf_{t} defined in Section 4 holds uniformly for integers 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T as η=τ/T→0\eta=\tau/T\to 0,

ft​(β)=(1−γ​η−γ2​η2​β1−β)t+O⁡(η2).f_{t}(\beta)=\left(1-\gamma\eta-\gamma^{2}\eta^{2}\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}\right)^{t}+O(\eta^{2}). (E.1)

Together with fT​(0)=(1−γ​η)Tf_{T}(0)=(1-\gamma\eta)^{T}, Lemma E.1 gives

fT​(0)−fT​(β)\displaystyle f_{T}(0)-f_{T}(\beta) =(1−γ​η)T−(1−γ​η−γ2​η2​β1−β)T+O⁡(η2)\displaystyle=(1-\gamma\eta)^{T}-\left(1-\gamma\eta-\gamma^{2}\eta^{2}\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}\right)^{T}+O(\eta^{2})
=T​γ2​η2​β1−β​(1−γ​η)T−1+O⁡(T2​η4+η2)\displaystyle=T\gamma^{2}\eta^{2}\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}(1-\gamma\eta)^{T-1}+O(T^{2}\eta^{4}+\eta^{2})
=γ2​τ​e−γ​τ​η​β1−β+O⁡(η2).\displaystyle=\gamma^{2}\tau e^{-\gamma\tau}\frac{\eta\beta}{1-\beta}+O(\eta^{2}). (E.2)

The second line is Taylor’s formula for the power. The last line uses T​η=τT\eta=\tau and (1−γ​η)T−1=e−γ​τ+O⁡(η)(1-\gamma\eta)^{T-1}=e^{-\gamma\tau}+O(\eta). Lemma E.1 and T​η=τT\eta=\tau give fT​(0)=e−γ​τ+O⁡(η)f_{T}(0)=e^{-\gamma\tau}+O(\eta) and fT​(β)=e−γ​τ+O⁡(η)f_{T}(\beta)=e^{-\gamma\tau}+O(\eta). To obtain the objective gain along the exact path, we integrate (B.6) from a=fT​(β)a=f_{T}(\beta) to a=fT​(0)a=f_{T}(0), which gives

J⁡(θTβ)−J⁡(θT0)\displaystyle J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})-J(\theta_{T}^{0}) =γ∫fT​(β)fT​(0)aVary∼πθ⋆+a⁡(θ0−θ⋆)(⋅∣x)[θ0(x,y)−θ⋆(x,y)]da\displaystyle=\gamma\int_{f_{T}(\beta)}^{f_{T}(0)}a\operatorname{Var}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta^{\star}+a(\theta_{0}-\theta^{\star})}(\cdot\mid x)}[\theta_{0}(x,y)-\theta^{\star}(x,y)]\,\mathrm{d}a
=γ​e−γ​τ​Vary∼πθ⋆+e−γ​τ​(θ0−θ⋆)​[θ0​(x,y)−θ⋆​(x,y)]​[fT​(0)−fT​(β)]+O⁡(η2)\displaystyle=\gamma e^{-\gamma\tau}\operatorname{Var}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta^{\star}+e^{-\gamma\tau}(\theta_{0}-\theta^{\star})}}[\theta_{0}(x,y)-\theta^{\star}(x,y)][f_{T}(0)-f_{T}(\beta)]+O(\eta^{2})
=C⁡(τ,γ)​η​β1−β+O⁡(η2).\displaystyle=C(\tau,\gamma)\frac{\eta\beta}{1-\beta}+O(\eta^{2}). (E.3)

The integrand varies by O⁡(η)O(\eta) over an interval of length O⁡(η)O(\eta), which explains the second-line remainder. The constant in Theorem 5.3 is given explicitly by

C(τ,γ)=γ3τe−2​γ​τVary∼πθ⋆+e−γ​τ​(θ0−θ⋆)(⋅∣x)[θ0(x,y)−θ⋆(x,y)].\displaystyle C(\tau,\gamma)=\gamma^{3}\tau e^{-2\gamma\tau}\operatorname{Var}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta^{\star}+e^{-\gamma\tau}(\theta_{0}-\theta^{\star})}(\cdot\mid x)}[\theta_{0}(x,y)-\theta^{\star}(x,y)]. (E.4)

This expression specifies its dependence on the problem, τ\tau, and γ\gamma. It is independent of η\eta, β\beta, and BB. The coefficient is strictly positive under the nondegeneracy condition, which implies θ0≠θ⋆\theta_{0}\neq\theta^{\star}.

Difference between the quadratic terms. Using ft​(0)=(1−γ​η)tf_{t}(0)=(1-\gamma\eta)^{t}, Lemma E.1 and the mean value theorem give |ft​(β)−ft​(0)|≤t​γ2​η2​β/(1−β)+O⁡(η2)=O⁡(η)|f_{t}(\beta)-f_{t}(0)|\leq t\gamma^{2}\eta^{2}\beta/(1-\beta)+O(\eta^{2})=O(\eta) uniformly for 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T, since t​η≤τt\eta\leq\tau. Lemma 4.1 then gives ‖θtβ−θt0‖∞=|ft​(β)−ft​(0)|⋅‖θ0−θ⋆‖∞\|\theta_{t}^{\beta}-\theta_{t}^{0}\|_{\infty}=|f_{t}(\beta)-f_{t}(0)|\cdot\|\theta_{0}-\theta^{\star}\|_{\infty}, and hence maxt≤T⁡‖θtβ−θt0‖∞=O⁡(η)\max_{t\leq T}\|\theta_{t}^{\beta}-\theta_{t}^{0}\|_{\infty}=O(\eta). Since J⁡(θ)J(\theta) is smooth and the entries of θtβ\theta_{t}^{\beta} and θt0\theta_{t}^{0} are bounded uniformly in t≤Tt\leq T and η\eta, ‖∇3J​(θ)‖op\|\nabla^{3}J(\theta)\|_{\mathrm{op}} is bounded independently of η\eta whenever the entries of θ\theta satisfy the same bound. This gives a Lipschitz bound for ∇2J​(θ)\nabla^{2}J(\theta) with a constant independent of η\eta. Combining this with the preceding O⁡(η)O(\eta) bound on the parameter difference gives ‖∇2J​(θTβ)−∇2J​(θT0)‖op=O⁡(η)\|\nabla^{2}J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})-\nabla^{2}J(\theta_{T}^{0})\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(\eta). To compare the two sampling corrections in Lemma 5.1, we also need the following bound on ΣTβ−ΣT0\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}-\Sigma_{T}^{0}.

Lemma E.2 (Covariance comparison).

Let ΣTβ\Sigma_{T}^{\beta} be defined by (C.4). For fixed β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1) and τ>0\tau>0, as η=τ/T→0\eta=\tau/T\to 0, we have ‖ΣTβ−ΣT0‖op=O⁡(η).\|\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}-\Sigma_{T}^{0}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(\eta).

Combining this bound with the preceding Hessian estimate, we obtain

|tr⁡[∇2J​(θTβ)​ΣTβ−∇2J​(θT0)​ΣT0]|\displaystyle\left|\operatorname{tr}[\nabla^{2}J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}-\nabla^{2}J(\theta_{T}^{0})\Sigma_{T}^{0}]\right|
≤|𝒴|⋅‖∇2J​(θTβ)−∇2J​(θT0)‖op⋅‖ΣTβ‖op+|𝒴|⋅‖∇2J​(θT0)‖op⋅‖ΣTβ−ΣT0‖op=O⁡(η).\displaystyle\quad\leq|\mathcal{Y}|\cdot\|\nabla^{2}J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})-\nabla^{2}J(\theta_{T}^{0})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\cdot\|\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+|\mathcal{Y}|\cdot\|\nabla^{2}J(\theta_{T}^{0})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\cdot\|\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}-\Sigma_{T}^{0}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(\eta).

Here we add and subtract ∇2J​(θT0)​ΣTβ\nabla^{2}J(\theta_{T}^{0})\Sigma_{T}^{\beta} inside the trace, then bound each trace in absolute value. The bounds in Appendix C give ‖ΣTβ‖op=O⁡(1)\|\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1) and ‖∇2J​(θT0)‖op=O⁡(1)\|\nabla^{2}J(\theta_{T}^{0})\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1). Lemma 5.1 and (E.3) therefore yield

𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})] =C⁡(τ,γ)​η​β1−β+O⁡(η2)+O⁡(η2/B)+O⁡((η/B)3/2)\displaystyle=C(\tau,\gamma)\frac{\eta\beta}{1-\beta}+O(\eta^{2})+O(\eta^{2}/B)+O((\eta/B)^{3/2})
=C⁡(τ,γ)​η​β1−β+O⁡(η3/2).\displaystyle=C(\tau,\gamma)\frac{\eta\beta}{1-\beta}+O(\eta^{3/2}).

Probability of improvement. The mean-to-standard-deviation ratio alone does not determine the winning probability. We also need the following normal limit to characterize the distribution of the objective difference, which is proved in the next subsection.

Lemma E.3 (Asymptotic normality).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 5.3, the distribution of the standardized objective difference converges to a standard normal distribution as η→0\eta\to 0,

J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)−𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]Std⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]→d𝒩⁡(0,1).\frac{J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})-\mathbb{E}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]}{\operatorname{Std}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{d}}\mathcal{N}(0,1). (E.5)

The mean expansion and Proposition 5.2 give 𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]/Std⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]→0\mathbb{E}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]/\operatorname{Std}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]\to 0. Combining this estimate with the normal limit in Lemma E.3 gives ℙ⁡(J⁡(θ^Tβ)>J⁡(θ^T0))→1/2\mathbb{P}(J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})>J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0}))\to 1/2. ∎

For the second inequality, we have ∑t′=0t−1∑ℓ=t′t−1ωβ​(ℓ,t′)=∑ℓ=0t−1∑t′=0ℓωβ​(ℓ,t′)=t\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{t-1}\sum_{\ell=t^{\prime}}^{t-1}\omega_{\beta}(\ell,t^{\prime})=\sum_{\ell=0}^{t-1}\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{\ell}\omega_{\beta}(\ell,t^{\prime})=t. maxt≤T⁡‖θtβ−θt0‖∞=maxt≤T⁡|ft​(β)−ft​(0)|⋅‖θ0−θ⋆‖∞=O⁡(η).\max_{t\leq T}\|\theta_{t}^{\beta}-\theta_{t}^{0}\|_{\infty}=\max_{t\leq T}|f_{t}(\beta)-f_{t}(0)|\cdot\|\theta_{0}-\theta^{\star}\|_{\infty}=O(\eta). (E.16)

Substituting (E.11), (E.15), and (E.16) into (E.10) yields ‖ΣTβ−ΣT0‖op=O⁡(η)\|\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}-\Sigma_{T}^{0}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(\eta). ∎

Proof of Lemma E.3.

We first analyze the centered objective difference for the auxiliary processes and then transfer the normal limit to the sampled processes.

Expansion of the auxiliary objective. Taylor’s formula at θTβ\theta_{T}^{\beta} gives J(θ~Tβ)=J(θTβ)+∇J(θTβ)⊤(θ~Tβ−θTβ)+RTβ,J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})=J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})+\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})^{\top}(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta}-\theta_{T}^{\beta})+R_{T}^{\beta}, where RTβR_{T}^{\beta} is the remainder after truncating this expansion at the linear term. Since 𝔼⁡[θ~Tβ]=θTβ\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta}]=\theta_{T}^{\beta} by Appendix C, the expected linear term is ∇J(θTβ)⊤(𝔼[θ~Tβ]−θTβ)=0\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})^{\top}(\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta}]-\theta_{T}^{\beta})=0. Subtracting expectations in the Taylor expansion gives

J(θ~Tβ)−𝔼[J(θ~Tβ)]=∇J(θTβ)⊤(θ~Tβ−θTβ)+RTβ−𝔼[RTβ].J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-\mathbb{E}[J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})]=\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})^{\top}(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta}-\theta_{T}^{\beta})+R_{T}^{\beta}-\mathbb{E}[R_{T}^{\beta}]. (E.17)

According to (C.3) and (C.6), we write the linear term as ∇J(θTβ)⊤(θ~Tβ−θTβ)=∑t=0T−1∑b=1BYt,bβ\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})^{\top}(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta}-\theta_{T}^{\beta})=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}Y_{t,b}^{\beta}, where Yt,bβ=Ψβ(T,t)𝟏{t<ζβ}∇J(θTβ)⊤εt,bβ/B.Y_{t,b}^{\beta}=\Psi_{\beta}(T,t)\mathbf{1}_{\{t<\zeta^{\beta}\}}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})^{\top}\varepsilon_{t,b}^{\beta}/B.

Normal limit for a single run. We next prove that (∑t=0T−1∑b=1BYt,bβ)/Std⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]→d𝒩⁡(0,1/2).(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}Y_{t,b}^{\beta})/\operatorname{Std}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]\xrightarrow{\mathrm{d}}\mathcal{N}(0,1/2). Let ℋt,b−1β\mathscr{H}_{t,b-1}^{\beta} denote the history before response bb at update tt, and reveal the T​BTB responses in increasing order of tt and then bb. Since 𝔼⁡[Yt,bβ∣ℋt,b−1β]=0\mathbb{E}[Y_{t,b}^{\beta}\mid\mathscr{H}_{t,b-1}^{\beta}]=0, these variables form a martingale difference sequence. We apply the martingale central limit theorem stated in Douc et al. (2018, Theorem E.4.1) to the partial sums of Yt,bβ/Std⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]Y_{t,b}^{\beta}/\operatorname{Std}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})] as T→∞T\to\infty. Using (C.1) and (C.4), we write the covariance replacement as

∑t=0T−1∑b=1B𝔼[(Yt,bβ)2∣ℋt,b−1β]−ηB∇J(θTβ)⊤ΣTβ∇J(θTβ)\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbb{E}[(Y_{t,b}^{\beta})^{2}\mid\mathscr{H}_{t,b-1}^{\beta}]-\frac{\eta}{B}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})^{\top}\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})
=∑t=0T−1∑b=1BΨβ(T,t)2𝟏{t<ζβ}B2∇J(θTβ)⊤[diag(𝐫πθ~tβ(⋅∣x))−𝐫𝐫⊤]∇J(θTβ)\displaystyle\quad=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\frac{\Psi_{\beta}(T,t)^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{t<\zeta^{\beta}\}}}{B^{2}}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})^{\top}\bigg[\operatorname{diag}\bigg(\frac{\mathbf{r}}{\pi_{\widetilde{\theta}_{t}^{\beta}}(\cdot\mid x)}\bigg)-\mathbf{r}\mathbf{r}^{\top}\bigg]\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})
−∑t=0T−1∑b=1BΨβ​(T,t)2B2∇J(θTβ)⊤[diag(𝐫πθtβ(⋅∣x))−𝐫𝐫⊤]∇J(θTβ)\displaystyle\qquad-\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\frac{\Psi_{\beta}(T,t)^{2}}{B^{2}}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})^{\top}\bigg[\operatorname{diag}\bigg(\frac{\mathbf{r}}{\pi_{\theta_{t}^{\beta}}(\cdot\mid x)}\bigg)-\mathbf{r}\mathbf{r}^{\top}\bigg]\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta}) (E.18)

The third inequality in (C.5) gives ∑t=0T−1∑b=1BΨβ​(T,t)2/B2≤5​τ​e2​γ​τ​η/B\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\Psi_{\beta}(T,t)^{2}/B^{2}\leq 5\tau e^{2\gamma\tau}\eta/B. Together with the boundedness of ∇J​(θTβ)\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta}), these bounds give an expected absolute value of O⁡((η/B)3/2)O((\eta/B)^{3/2}) for the right-hand side. For the term ∇J(θTβ)⊤ΣTβ∇J(θTβ)\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})^{\top}\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta}), the difference between the EMA and no-EMA versions can be bounded by

|∇J(θTβ)⊤ΣTβ∇J(θTβ)−∇J(θT0)⊤ΣT0∇J(θT0)|\displaystyle\big|\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})^{\top}\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})-\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{0})^{\top}\Sigma_{T}^{0}\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{0})\big| (E.19)
≤‖∇J​(θTβ)−∇J​(θT0)‖2⋅‖ΣTβ‖op​(‖∇J​(θTβ)‖2+‖∇J​(θT0)‖2)\displaystyle\quad\leq\|\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})-\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{0})\|_{2}\cdot\|\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\big(\|\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})\|_{2}+\|\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{0})\|_{2}\big)
+∥∇J(θT0)∥22⋅∥ΣTβ−ΣT0∥op=O(η).\displaystyle\qquad+\|\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{0})\|_{2}^{2}\cdot\|\Sigma_{T}^{\beta}-\Sigma_{T}^{0}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(\eta). (E.20)

Lemma E.2, the parameter difference bound (E.16), the Lipschitz continuity of ∇J​(θ)\nabla J(\theta) and the boundedness of ∇J​(θ)\nabla J(\theta) and ΣTβ\Sigma_{T}^{\beta} give the last bound. According to Proposition 5.2, Var⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]\operatorname{Var}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})] is Θ⁡(η/B)\Theta(\eta/B). The expected absolute value of the right-hand side of (E.18) divided by this variance is O⁡(η/B)O(\sqrt{\eta/B}). Markov’s inequality therefore gives convergence in probability to zero. The difference (E.20) gives the limit 1/21/2. To apply the martingale central limit theorem, we also need to bound the conditional second moments ∑t=0T−1∑b=1B𝔼[(Yt,bβ)2𝟏{|Yt,bβ|>ϵStd[J(θ^Tβ)−J(θ^T0)]}∣ℋt,b−1β]\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbb{E}\big[(Y_{t,b}^{\beta})^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_{t,b}^{\beta}|>\epsilon\operatorname{Std}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]\}}\mid\mathscr{H}_{t,b-1}^{\beta}\big], where ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is a fixed constant. The definition of Yt,bβY_{t,b}^{\beta} gives

maxt<T,b≤B⁡|Yt,bβ|\displaystyle\max_{t<T,\,b\leq B}|Y_{t,b}^{\beta}| ≤‖∇J​(θTβ)‖2Bmaxt<T,b≤B(|Ψβ(T,t)|⋅∥𝟏{t<ζβ}εt,bβ∥2)\displaystyle\leq\frac{\|\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})\|_{2}}{B}\max_{t<T,\,b\leq B}\big(|\Psi_{\beta}(T,t)|\cdot\|\mathbf{1}_{\{t<\zeta^{\beta}\}}\varepsilon_{t,b}^{\beta}\|_{2}\big)
≤|𝒴|​L​eγ​τ​ηB​‖∇J​(θTβ)‖2​max⁡∑k=tT−1t<T⁡ωβ​(k,t)\displaystyle\leq\frac{\sqrt{|\mathcal{Y}|}Le^{\gamma\tau}\eta}{B}\|\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})\|_{2}\max_{t<T}\sum_{k=t}^{T-1}\omega_{\beta}(k,t)
≤|𝒴|​L​eγ​τ​ηB⁡(1−β)​‖∇J​(θTβ)‖2=O⁡(η/B).\displaystyle\leq\frac{\sqrt{|\mathcal{Y}|}Le^{\gamma\tau}\eta}{B(1-\beta)}\|\nabla J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})\|_{2}=O(\eta/B).

The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives the first line. The second inequality uses the stopped noise bound ∥𝟏{t<ζβ}εt,bβ∥∞≤L\|\mathbf{1}_{\{t<\zeta^{\beta}\}}\varepsilon_{t,b}^{\beta}\|_{\infty}\leq L in Appendix C and the first line of (C.20). (∑t=0T−1∑b=1B𝔼[(Yt,bβ)2𝟏{|Yt,bβ|>ϵStd[J(θ^Tβ)−J(θ^T0)]}∣ℋt,b−1β])/Var[J(θ^Tβ)−J(θ^T0)]→ℙ0.\Big(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbb{E}\big[(Y_{t,b}^{\beta})^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_{t,b}^{\beta}|>\epsilon\operatorname{Std}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]\}}\mid\mathscr{H}_{t,b-1}^{\beta}\big]\Big)/\operatorname{Var}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0. (E.22)

Here we use maxt<T,b≤B⁡|Yt,bβ|/Std⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]=O⁡(η/B)→0\max_{t<T,\,b\leq B}|Y_{t,b}^{\beta}|/\operatorname{Std}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]=O(\sqrt{\eta/B})\to 0. Thus for each fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0, every indicator is zero for all sufficiently small η\eta. Equations (E.21) and (E.22) verify the two conditions of the theorem with limiting variance 1/21/2, giving

(∑t=0T−1∑b=1BYt,bβ)/Std⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]→d𝒩⁡(0,1/2).\Big(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{b=1}^{B}Y_{t,b}^{\beta}\Big)/\operatorname{Std}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]\xrightarrow{\mathrm{d}}\mathcal{N}(0,1/2). (E.23)

Distribution of J⁡(θ~Tβ)−𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ~Tβ)]J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-\mathbb{E}[J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})]. The remainder in the Taylor expansion (E.17) satisfies |RTβ|≤sup‖ϑ‖∞≤M+L​τ​eγ​τ‖∇2J​(ϑ)‖op⋅‖θ~Tβ−θTβ‖22/2|R_{T}^{\beta}|\leq\sup_{\|\vartheta\|_{\infty}\leq M+L\tau e^{\gamma\tau}}\|\nabla^{2}J(\vartheta)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\cdot\|\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta}-\theta_{T}^{\beta}\|_{2}^{2}/2, where MM and LL are constants defined in Appendix C. Therefore, (C.10) gives 𝔼​|RTβ−𝔼⁡[RTβ]|≤2​𝔼|RTβ|=O⁡(η/B)\mathbb{E}|R_{T}^{\beta}-\mathbb{E}[R_{T}^{\beta}]|\leq 2\mathbb{E}|R_{T}^{\beta}|=O(\eta/B). Dividing by Std⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]\operatorname{Std}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})] and applying Markov’s inequality gives |RTβ−𝔼⁡[RTβ]|/Std⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]→ℙ0|R_{T}^{\beta}-\mathbb{E}[R_{T}^{\beta}]|/\operatorname{Std}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0. Applying Slutsky’s theorem (Kroese and Botev, 2023, Chapter 3, Exercise 31) to (E.17), using (E.23) and the remainder bound above, gives (J⁡(θ~Tβ)−𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ~Tβ)])/Std⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]→d𝒩⁡(0,1/2).(J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-\mathbb{E}[J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})])/\operatorname{Std}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]\xrightarrow{\mathrm{d}}\mathcal{N}(0,1/2). The same argument holds for the no-EMA run. Combining the two independent limits gives

J⁡(θ~Tβ)−J⁡(θ~T0)−𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ~Tβ)−J⁡(θ~T0)]Std⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]→d𝒩⁡(0,1).\frac{J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{0})-\mathbb{E}[J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{0})]}{\operatorname{Std}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{d}}\mathcal{N}(0,1). (E.24)

Transfer to the sampled processes. As the auxiliary process and the sampled process differ only after the exit time, we have

𝔼​|J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ~Tβ)|≤2​supθ|J⁡(θ)|​ℙ​(ζβ≤T)=o⁡(η/B).\mathbb{E}|J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})|\leq 2\sup_{\theta}|J(\theta)|\,\mathbb{P}(\zeta^{\beta}\leq T)=o(\sqrt{\eta/B}). (E.25)

Here we use the exit probability bound in (C.9) and −γ​log⁡(1/miny⁡πref​(y∣x))≤J⁡(θ)≤1-\gamma\log(1/\min_{y}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x))\leq J(\theta)\leq 1. The centered discrepancy satisfies 𝔼​|J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ~Tβ)−𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ~Tβ)]|≤2​𝔼|J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ~Tβ)|=o⁡(η/B)\mathbb{E}|J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-\mathbb{E}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})]|\leq 2\mathbb{E}|J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})|=o(\sqrt{\eta/B}). Since the standard deviation is Θ⁡(η/B)\Theta(\sqrt{\eta/B}) by Proposition 5.2, Markov’s inequality gives

J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ~Tβ)−𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ~Tβ)]Std⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]→ℙ0.\displaystyle\frac{J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-\mathbb{E}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widetilde{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})]}{\operatorname{Std}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0. (E.26)

The same estimate holds when β=0\beta=0. Slutsky’s theorem therefore transfers the standard normal limit to the standardized difference of the sampled objectives. ∎

Appendix F Vanishing expected gain as η/(1−β)→0\eta/(1-\beta)\to 0

We formalize and prove the vanishing expected gain claim at the beginning of Section 5.2.

Lemma F.1 (Vanishing expected gain).

Fix B≥1B\geq 1 and τ>0\tau>0, and consider the two runs in Section 5. For any deterministic β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1), possibly depending on η\eta, if η/(1−β)→0\eta/(1-\beta)\to 0 as η=τ/T→0\eta=\tau/T\to 0, then the expected gain satisfies 𝔼⁡[J⁡(θ^Tβ)−J⁡(θ^T0)]→0\mathbb{E}[J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{\beta})-J(\widehat{\theta}_{T}^{0})]\to 0 as η→0\eta\to 0.

Proof.

We first bound the exact gain and then control the sampling correction.

Exact difference. Subtracting the definitions of fT​(β)f_{T}(\beta) and fT​(0)f_{T}(0) in Section 4 gives

|fT​(β)−fT​(0)|\displaystyle|f_{T}(\beta)-f_{T}(0)| =|(1−γ​η)​(fT−1​(β)−fT−1​(0))−γ​η​∑t′=0T−1ωβ​(T−1,t′)​(ft′​(β)−fT−1​(β))|\displaystyle=\big|(1-\gamma\eta)\big(f_{T-1}(\beta)-f_{T-1}(0)\big)-\gamma\eta\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{T-1}\omega_{\beta}(T-1,t^{\prime})\big(f_{t^{\prime}}(\beta)-f_{T-1}(\beta)\big)\big|
=γ​η​|∑t=0T−1(1−γ​η)T−t−1​∑t′=0tωβ​(t,t′)​(ft′​(β)−ft​(β))|\displaystyle=\gamma\eta\big|\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}(1-\gamma\eta)^{T-t-1}\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{t}\omega_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime})\big(f_{t^{\prime}}(\beta)-f_{t}(\beta)\big)\big|
≤γ2​η2​eγ​τ​∑t=0T−1∑t′=0t(t−t′)​ωβ​(t,t′)≤γ2​τ​eγ​τ​η​β/(1−β).\displaystyle\leq\gamma^{2}\eta^{2}e^{\gamma\tau}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{t}(t-t^{\prime})\omega_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime})\leq\gamma^{2}\tau e^{\gamma\tau}\eta\beta/(1-\beta). (F.1)

The first line uses ∑t′=0T−1ωβ​(T−1,t′)=1\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{T-1}\omega_{\beta}(T-1,t^{\prime})=1 to add γ​η​∑t′=0T−1ωβ​(T−1,t′)​fT−1​(β)\gamma\eta\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{T-1}\omega_{\beta}(T-1,t^{\prime})f_{T-1}(\beta) and subtract γ​η​fT−1​(β)\gamma\eta f_{T-1}(\beta). Repeatedly substituting this relation and using f0​(β)=f0​(0)=1f_{0}(\beta)=f_{0}(0)=1 yields the second line. The definition of ft​(β)f_{t}(\beta) and the bound |ft​(β)|≤eγ​τ|f_{t}(\beta)|\leq e^{\gamma\tau} in Lemma C.1 give |ft′​(β)−ft​(β)|≤γ​η​eγ​τ​(t−t′)|f_{t^{\prime}}(\beta)-f_{t}(\beta)|\leq\gamma\eta e^{\gamma\tau}(t-t^{\prime}). Applying (1−γ​η)T−t−1≤1(1-\gamma\eta)^{T-t-1}\leq 1, T​η=τT\eta=\tau and ∑t′=0t(t−t′)​ωβ​(t,t′)≤β/(1−β)\sum_{t^{\prime}=0}^{t}(t-t^{\prime})\omega_{\beta}(t,t^{\prime})\leq\beta/(1-\beta), which follows by summing the weights defined in Section 3, gives the last line. For the objective difference, we have

|J⁡(θTβ)−J⁡(θT0)|≤sup‖θ‖∞≤M‖∇J​(θ)‖2⋅‖θTβ−θT0‖2≤γ2​τ​eγ​τ​η​β​‖θ0−θ⋆‖2​sup‖θ‖∞≤M‖∇J​(θ)‖21−β.\displaystyle|J(\theta_{T}^{\beta})-J(\theta_{T}^{0})|\leq\sup_{\|\theta\|_{\infty}\leq M}\|\nabla J(\theta)\|_{2}\cdot\|\theta_{T}^{\beta}-\theta_{T}^{0}\|_{2}\leq\frac{\gamma^{2}\tau e^{\gamma\tau}\eta\beta\|\theta_{0}-\theta^{\star}\|_{2}\sup_{\|\theta\|_{\infty}\leq M}\|\nabla J(\theta)\|_{2}}{1-\beta}.

The first inequality follows from the mean value theorem. The second inequality uses Lemma 4.1 to express ‖θTβ−θT0‖2\|\theta_{T}^{\beta}-\theta_{T}^{0}\|_{2} in terms of |fT​(β)−fT​(0)||f_{T}(\beta)-f_{T}(0)| and applies (F.1). We first match the exact endpoints at finite step size. In this section, fT​(η,β)f_{T}(\eta,\beta) displays the learning-rate argument because the two runs use different rates.

We pass to the continuous covariance, compute its long-time limit, and control relative error.
